Laboratory populations of Caenorhabditis briggsae maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] display a remarkably brief developmental interval from egg deposition to hatching, with the age at birth recorded as 13/24 of a day (13/24 d) [ab = 13/24 d]. This rapid embryogenesis, completing in just over half a day, is characteristic of fast-growing rhabditid nematodes and allows newly hatched first-stage larvae to commence exogenous feeding almost immediately after emerging from the egg. Freshly emerged individuals carry a minimal body mass at birth of 0.025 micrograms [Wwb = 0.025 micrograms], a value reflecting the modest cytoplasmic reserves allocated to each fertilised ovum. The subsequent growth trajectory is strongly modulated by resource availability, as demonstrated by controlled feeding experiments. When reared on an abundant bacterial lawn, populations achieve their ultimate wet weight at high food conditions, reaching approximately 0.928 micrograms [Wwi = approximately 0.928 micrograms] as fully grown adults. This substantial mass gain, representing a greater than thirty-fold increase over the neonatal weight, underscores the capacity for rapid somatic expansion when nutritional constraints are minimal.

Under restricted dietary regimes, the same species exhibits a markedly different growth outcome, attaining an ultimate wet weight at low food of only 0.39 micrograms [Wwi = 0.39 micrograms]. This value highlights the extreme plasticity inherent in nematode body size determination, where adult mass can be reduced by more than half when bacterial food supplies are limiting. Such plasticity carries direct consequences for the timing of reproductive maturation. Individuals raised on sparse food rations typically become reproductively mature at a wet weight at puberty at low food of 0.204 micrograms [Wwp = 0.204 micrograms], a threshold that is reached after a prolonged period of slow, incremental growth. In contrast, well-fed cohorts, enjoying continuous access to a rich bacterial substrate, undergo pubertal development at a substantially larger body size, with the wet weight at puberty at high food averaging 0.404 micrograms [Wwp = 0.404 micrograms]. This nearly twofold difference in mass at the onset of reproduction illustrates how nutritional history directly governs the allocation of resources toward gonadal development versus continued somatic growth during the juvenile and sub-adult phases.

Life span in this species is similarly constrained by the thermal regime, with experimental cohorts incubated at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] exhibiting a maximum recorded longevity of 16 days [am = 16 days]. This relatively short life cycle, spanning from emergent larva to senescent adult in little more than two weeks, positions Caenorhabditis briggsae among the faster-lived members of its genus. The brevity of adult life is partially offset by an intense period of reproductive activity that commences soon after the pubertal mass thresholds are crossed. Observations of individual worms suggest that the post-pubertal phase is characterised by a rapid succession of egg-laying events, with gravid hermaphrodites producing clutches over several consecutive days before entering a gradual, post-reproductive decline. Physiological deterioration in late life manifests as a progressive loss of pharyngeal pumping efficiency and a marked reduction in locomotion, culminating in natural mortality shortly after the reproductive window has closed.

Comparative studies between low-food and high-food rearing conditions reveal that the trajectories toward both ultimate mass and pubertal mass are tightly coupled to ingestion rate. Under high food, the ultimate wet weight at high food of 0.928 micrograms [Wwi = 0.928 micrograms] is attained with a corresponding wet weight at puberty at high food of 0.404 micrograms [Wwp = 0.404 micrograms], indicating that roughly forty-three percent of the final adult mass is achieved by the time gonadal maturation occurs. By contrast, under low food, the wet weight at puberty at low food of 0.204 micrograms [Wwp = 0.204 micrograms] represents over half of the low-food ultimate wet weight at low food of 0.39 micrograms [Wwi = 0.39 micrograms], suggesting that when resources are scarce, a greater relative fraction of growth must be completed before the organism commits to reproduction. This shift in the proportion of mass dedicated to pre-pubertal development likely reflects an adaptive strategy to ensure that individuals attain a minimum viable size before investing in offspring, even under energetically adverse circumstances.

The consistency of these life-history parameters across repeated experimental trials underscores the reliability of Caenorhabditis briggsae as a model for studying resource-dependent growth and reproduction. At the standard laboratory temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a lifespan of 16 days [am = 16 days] and an embryonic period of 13/24 of a day (13/24 d) [ab = 13/24 d] have been documented repeatedly, forming a stable baseline for comparative work with related species such as Caenorhabditis elegans. The birth mass of 0.025 micrograms [Wwb = 0.025 micrograms] serves as a critical starting point for energy budget calculations, while the contrast between ultimate wet weight at low food of 0.39 micrograms [Wwi = 0.39 micrograms] and ultimate wet weight at high food of 0.928 micrograms [Wwi = 0.928 micrograms] provides a clear demonstration of phenotypic plasticity in adult body size. Similarly, the divergence between wet weight at puberty at low food of 0.204 micrograms [Wwp = 0.204 micrograms] and wet weight at puberty at high food of 0.404 micrograms [Wwp = 0.404 micrograms] highlights how nutritional conditions can shift the developmental schedule and the size threshold for reproductive competence in this free-living nematode.
